```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4.5)
```

```{r load}
library(mirt)
library(irtident)
```

## A 3PL example

mirt summarises the conditioning of the whole model with the condition number of the information matrix:

```{r fit}
dat <- expand.table(LSAT7)
fit <- mirt(dat, 1, itemtype = "3PL", SE = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)
extract.mirt(fit, "secondordertest")
extract.mirt(fit, "condnum")
```

irtident breaks this down by item and parameter.

## Combined diagnostics

```{r diagnose}
set.seed(1)
dx <- id_diagnose(fit, n_starts = 8)
dx
```

Four of the five items have a guessing parameter at its lower bound: for them the data are consistent with a 2PL item. Item 2's guessing parameter is estimated at about 0.3, but it is associated with the intercept, and the data cannot rule out `g = 0`.

The diagnosis combines three pieces of evidence, described below.

## 1. Local diagnostics: where does the uncertainty come from?

`id_local()` splits each parameter's sampling variance into three factors:

$$SE_j^2 = SE_{cond,j}^2 \times VIF^{within}_j \times VIF^{between}_j$$

* $SE_{cond,j}$: the standard error if every other parameter were known (how much information the data carry about this parameter alone);
* $VIF^{within}_j$: inflation from not knowing the other parameters *of the same item*;
* $VIF^{between}_j$: inflation from not knowing the parameters of *other items* and of the latent distribution.

```{r local}
loc <- dx$local
p <- loc$params[loc$params$item == "Item.2",
                c("param", "value", "se", "se_cond", "vif_within", "vif_between")]
p
```

For item 2, the within-item variance inflation factors of `g` and `d` are about 20: their standard errors are about $\sqrt{20} \approx 4.5$ times what they would be if the other parameters of item 2 were known. Standard errors of `g` are on the logit scale.

The eigenvectors of the scaled information matrix with small eigenvalues give the directions along which the log-likelihood is nearly flat:

```{r directions}
loc$directions
```

`g` and `d` load with opposite signs: raising the guessing parameter while lowering the intercept leaves the fit almost unchanged.

### Guessing parameters in easy items

Consider a 3PL test with `a = 1.5` and `g = 0.2` for every item and a range of difficulties. The following code evaluates expected (Fisher) information at the generating values. The information depends on those values and N; the simulated data provide the mirt object used for the calculation.

```{r sim}
set.seed(2026)
n_items <- 12
b <- seq(-2.5, 2.5, length.out = n_items)
sim <- simdata(matrix(1.5, n_items), matrix(-1.5 * b), N = 3000,
               itemtype = "3PL", guess = 0.2)
pv <- mirt(sim, 1, itemtype = "3PL", pars = "values")
pv$value[pv$name == "a1"] <- 1.5
pv$value[pv$name == "d"] <- -1.5 * b
pv$value[pv$name == "g"] <- 0.2
at_truth <- mirt(sim, 1, itemtype = "3PL", pars = pv, TOL = NaN,
                 verbose = FALSE)
loc_truth <- id_local(at_truth, SE.type = "Fisher")
g_rows <- loc_truth$params[loc_truth$params$name == "g", ]
round(data.frame(b = b, se = g_rows$se, se_cond = g_rows$se_cond,
                 vif_within = g_rows$vif_within), 2)
```

```{r sim-plot, fig.height = 4}
plot(b, g_rows$se, log = "y", pch = 19, type = "b",
     xlab = "item difficulty b", ylab = "SE of logit(g), log scale",
     main = "Precision of guessing estimates by item difficulty (N = 3000)")
```

The lower asymptote is most evident at low ability relative to item difficulty. For easy items, few respondents occupy that region. In this example, easy items have less conditional information about `g` and greater within-item confounding with the intercept.

## 2. Profile likelihood: is the interval closed?

`id_profile()` fixes a parameter at a grid of values, re-estimates everything else, and records the deviance. A parameter is practically identified when its profile likelihood interval is closed on both sides (Raue et al., 2009).

```{r profile}
dx$profile
```

```{r profile-plot, fig.height = 5}
plot(dx, params = c("Item.1:g", "Item.2:g", "Item.4:g", "Item.2:a1"))
```

For `Item.2:g` the Wald interval excludes 0, but the profile interval reaches it: the quadratic approximation behind the Wald interval does not describe this profile well. For `Item.1:g`, the profile stays below the cutoff from 0 to 0.5.

At a bound of the parameter space (`g = 0`, `u = 1`), the deviance is compared with the cutoff of the 50:50 mixture of $\chi^2_0$ and $\chi^2_1$ (Self & Liang, 1987):

```{r cutoffs}
c(interior = dx$profile$cutoff, bound = dx$profile$cutoff_bound)
```

## 3. Multiple starting values

`id_multistart()` refits from random starting values and clusters the solutions. Clusters that reach the same log-likelihood with different parameter values are reported as equivalent fit; clusters with a lower log-likelihood as inferior optima. For example:

```{r multistart}
fit4 <- mirt(dat, 1, itemtype = "4PL", verbose = FALSE)
set.seed(2)
ms <- id_multistart(fit4, n_starts = 6)
ms
```

## 4. Parameter precision across sample sizes

`id_samplesize()` simulates from the fitted model at several sample sizes, refits, and compares repeated-estimate SD with the SEs reported by mirt. It is run separately from `id_diagnose()`:

```{r samplesize, eval = FALSE}
set.seed(1)
ss <- id_samplesize(fit, params = c("Item.2:g", "Item.2:a1"),
                    N = c(1000, 2000, 4000, 8000), reps = 20)
ss
plot(ss)
```

For each parameter and N, the summary reports:

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `current` | Estimate from the original fitted model |
| `mean` | Mean of the repeated estimates |
| `sd` | SD of the repeated estimates |
| `mirt_se` | Root mean squared mirt SE, `sqrt(mean(SE^2))` |
| `n_used` | Replications used for the mean, SD and mirt SE |
| `success` | Successful fits divided by all attempted fits |
| `conv` | Converged fits divided by all attempted fits |
| `se_failure` | Fraction of converged successful fits without a usable estimate/SE pair |

The mean, SD and mirt SE use the same replications: converged fits with a finite estimate and a finite, positive SE for that parameter. Raw estimates and reporting-scale SEs are in `ss$estimates` and `ss$standard_errors`.

`plot(ss)` draws the SD and mirt SE against N.

For `g` and `u`, both use the probability scale; the logit SE from mirt is converted with the delta method, `p * (1 - p) * SE_logit`. SEs are evaluated at the converged estimates with the same fitting arguments; `SE.type` selects the mirt SE method. The `truth` argument sets the generating model and defaults to `fit`.

## Running in parallel

All diagnostics that refit the model accept `parallel = TRUE` and then use `future.apply` with whatever `future::plan()` is active:

```{r parallel, eval = FALSE}
future::plan(future::multisession, workers = 4)
dx <- id_diagnose(fit, parallel = TRUE)
```

## Supported models

* Unidimensional, single-group models from `mirt::mirt()`.
* Itemtypes `Rasch`, `2PL`, `3PL`, `3PLu`, `4PL` and `graded`.
* No equality constraints.

## References

Chalmers, R. P. (2012). mirt: A multidimensional item response theory package for the R environment. *Journal of Statistical Software, 48*(6), 1-29.

Raue, A., Kreutz, C., Maiwald, T., Bachmann, J., Schilling, M., Klingmuller, U., & Timmer, J. (2009). Structural and practical identifiability analysis of partially observed dynamical models by exploiting the profile likelihood. *Bioinformatics, 25*(15), 1923-1929.

Self, S. G., & Liang, K.-Y. (1987). Asymptotic properties of maximum likelihood estimators and likelihood ratio tests under nonstandard conditions. *Journal of the American Statistical Association, 82*(398), 605-610.
